reelection.rule: Rule: end of the current class term in legislators-current.yaml. Class 1 ends 2031-01-03. The November before that January 3 end is November 2030. The file does not store the election day, so no day of the month is shown.

vote_frequency.label: In this cached set only (the latest 40 Senate votes, not a lifetime record): 40 of 40. Yea or Aye: 30. Nay or No: 9. Not Voting: 1. Of 39 Yea or Nay votes where the Republican majority could be computed, 37 (95%) matched that majority (majority = the side most of that party's members voting Yea or Nay took; on average 51 members of that party voted Yea or Nay per roll call).

stands_for.caption: Grouped by Congress.gov's official policy area. Shows how they voted, not why. Final-passage, amendment, and procedural votes can mean different things; read the note for each.
stands_for.scope: Senate votes 1–262 of the 119th Congress, session 2 (262 votes, January 5, 2026 to November 12, 2026), from the Senate LIS.
stands_for.majority_rule: Party majority = the Yea/Nay side taken by most members of that party who voted Yea or Nay on that roll call, counted from the party code in the roll-call XML (all members, including ones no longer serving). Ties have no majority.
stands_for.factual_flag: Not yet summarized: this line is built only from the official vote question and the bill's official title.

said_voted.caption: Posts are shown as written. A post is matched to a vote only when it names the bill number or the bill's official title. A post can mention a bill for many reasons.
said_voted.topic_caption: Recent posts grouped by simple keyword rules that are identical for every member (published at /x_topic_rules.json). A post listed under a topic is not claimed to be about any specific vote; a post can appear under more than one topic.

Great work from @SecScottBessent and @SecRubio, who spearheaded important new chip restrictions on China. The new rules will:
 
✅Cut China's remote access to advanced chips through data centers around the world

✅Combat chip smuggling, particularly through Southeast Asia

✅Reduce China's ability to manufacture chips abroad
 
These overdue steps will play a critical role in closing loopholes that Megaspeed exploited to undermine the President's policy of restricting our best chips to China.

It's now on Congress to codify and build on these controls. Congress must include bipartisan, complementary bills in the NDAA this year that collectively will cut off the primary pathways through which China accesses chips.
 
AI Overwatch Act: My legislation with @SenWarren to codify President Trump's clear redline to block cutting-edge chips to China.

Chip Security Act: @SenTomCotton and @SenatorHassan bill to crack down on chip smuggling through location verification.

Remote Access Security Act: @SenMcCormickPA and @RonWyden legislation to cut off China's ability to rent cloud access to advance chips.

MATCH Act: @SenatorRicketts and @SenatorAndyKim bill to align allied controls to block China's ability to manufacture their own advanced chips

The time for debate is over. It’s our responsibility to get these bills into law this year and cut off China’s ability to access cutting-edge chips.

The AI race with China is all about who has the best and most chips. There are four main ways China gets access to chips:

1.) Buying them directly from US companies like Nvidia.

2.) Illegally smuggling them from other countries into China.

3.) Accessing them remotely through the cloud from data centers located in places like Southeast Asia.

4.) Building their own domestic chips in China.

The Chinese military has used advanced chips to further its capabilities while undermining our national security, and the Chinese government has used these chips to strengthen its totalitarian surveillance project.

Congress has a generational opportunity in this year’s NDAA to pass bipartisan bills that would address all four of the pathways through which China acquires chips.

While we need a full assessment of the damage done to our national security by recent revelations, we can begin today by setting a better course.

No excuses. No apologies. Let’s get this done.

conflicts.caption: These are overlaps in public records, not evidence of a deal. Lobbying can be for or against a bill, and donors' employers didn't necessarily give money.
conflicts.method: Each itemized donor dollar is counted once, under the industry of the donor's self-reported employer; an industry counts if at least one LD-2 client in it lobbied on any bill this member sponsored or voted on.

bills.vote_scope: Senate votes 1–262 of the 119th Congress, session 2 (262 votes, January 5, 2026 to November 12, 2026), from the Senate LIS.

overlap.cycle_note: Fallback cycle: these figures are from the 2024 two-year cycle (most recent completed election), not the current 2030 cycle. The 2030 cycle has no itemized donors yet.
